explanation:
## The program

```cpp
long long power(int base, int exponent = 2)
{
    long long result{ 1 };
    for (int i = 0; i < exponent; ++i) result *= base;
    return result;
}

std::cout << "square " << power(base) << "\n";
std::cout << "power " << power(base, exponent) << "\n";
```

## The default is part of the declaration, not the body

The `= 2` is not a statement that runs; it is information the
compiler uses at the **call site** to fill in the missing argument.
So it belongs wherever the caller can see it:

```cpp
long long power(int base, int exponent = 2);    // declaration

long long power(int base, int exponent)         // definition — no = 2
{
    /* ... */
}
```

Repeating the default on both is an error: "default argument given
for parameter 2 of ...". In a real project the declaration lives in
a header and the definition in a `.cpp`, which makes the rule read
naturally — the header is what callers read, so the default goes
there.

## Defaults fill from the right

```cpp
void f(int a, int b = 1, int c = 2);     // fine
void g(int a = 1, int b);                // error
```

Arguments are matched by position, so a gap in the middle would be
unreadable: `g(5)` could not say whether 5 was `a` or `b`. C++ has
no named arguments to resolve it with, so the rule is simply that
every parameter after a defaulted one must also be defaulted.

## Starting at the identity

`result` starts at 1 because 1 is what leaves a product unchanged.
The same reasoning as 0 for a sum, and it pays off at the edge:
`power(n, 0)` runs the body zero times and returns 1, which is the
conventional answer, without a branch.

`power(0, 0)` returns 1 here as well. That is a definition rather
than a fact — 0⁰ is genuinely ambiguous in analysis, and is taken as
1 in combinatorics and in most programming libraries because it
makes formulas come out. `std::pow(0.0, 0.0)` is also 1. The
statement says so rather than leaving the reader to discover which
convention the tests used.

## Why the return type is wider than the arguments

20 and 12 both fit in an `int` with room to spare; 20¹² does not.
The size of the inputs says nothing about the size of the output,
and multiplication is where that gap opens fastest. `result` is a
`long long` from the start, so every `*=` is a 64-bit multiply —
declaring it `int` and returning it into a `long long` would
overflow before the conversion, the same mistake as dividing in
`int`s and assigning to a `double`.

## What this does not check

Negative exponents, which the constraints exclude — the loop would
run zero times and return 1, when the right answer is not an integer
at all. A general `power` would either reject them or return a
`double`.
